title: Subject, Object(ive)
author: Jerilyn Olson
summary: Jerilyn Olson, Chief People Officer of Great Hearts, asks whether lesson objectives belong in classical education or are a technocratic import, and answers that they do belong if rightly ordered. She acknowledges the unease: the modern objective descends from Ralph Tyler, Bloom, and behaviorist 'SWBAT' formulas that can reduce the soul to measurables. Drawing on Aristotle's archer and Plato's image of lesser stones supporting greater ones, she reframes objectives as short-term aims serving the larger end of forming a person who knows the true, loves the good, and delights in the beautiful. Planning should therefore begin with the purpose of the discipline and the formation of the student, working down to units and lessons, with state standards serving as a floor rather than a ceiling. She adds three refinements: objectives should include what students should love and attend to, not only know and do; they should free teachers to guide responsive conversation like a hiking guide; and they usually belong in the lesson plan rather than on the whiteboard, since classical pedagogy moves from a concrete encounter to naming the universal. Her closing formula is 'discover first and label later.'
points: Olson traces lesson objectives to Tyler's 1949 curriculum principles and behaviorist SWBAT formulas, explaining classical teachers' suspicion of them.
Aristotle's archer image supports objectives as aims, provided the real question is whether daily aims are ordered to the proper end of education.
Classical planning should begin with the discipline's purpose and the student's formation, then descend to course, unit, week, and lesson.
A classical objective should name what affections a lesson should awaken and what habits of attention it strengthens, as illustrated by rethinking year-long K-2 poetry recitation goals.
Posting objectives up front can 'give away the punchline'; lessons should start with a concrete encounter and let students discover before the concept is labeled.
quotes: It came into focus in 1949, when Ralph Tyler published Basic Principles of Curriculum and Instruction and argued that curricula should be built around clear, intentional targets (borrowing language from military contexts). Benjamin Bloom and others then gave schools a standardized vocabulary for educational goals, while the influence of behaviorism coached teachers to define success primarily as observable, measurable action – especially with the rigid formula of SWBAT (“students will be able to”).

We fundamentally believe that the purpose of education is not the production of isolated performances, especially on standardized exams. The end of education is the cultivation of excellence in the human person: a soul learning to know what is true, love what is good, and delight in what is beautiful.

The question, then, is not whether we have objectives, but whether our aims are ordered to a proper end. Backwards planning is genuinely helpful, provided we are honest about the end from which we are working backwards. It forces a teacher to ask where the lesson is going before she gathers materials, invents an activity, or writes a clever question. But if the endpoint is only a quiz or standardized assessment, the lesson bends toward something too small. Assessment itself must serve a higher purpose.

In our planning, we begin not with the state standard, not with the activity, not even with the assessment. We begin with the purpose of the discipline and the formation of the student. From there we work down to the course, the unit, the week, and finally the lesson.

A classical lesson objective should ask not only what students will produce or perform, but what they should know, what they should be able to do, and what proper loves or affections might be awakened. The teacher must triangulate these aims as she shapes content, activity, and assessment. In planning, the teacher must ask: What should this lesson invite students to love?

The Latin obiectum refers to that which is placed before the mind or presented to sight. In the medieval and classical philosophical tradition, an object is not an independent target existing apart from the knower; it is that toward which the power of knowing is directed. For this reason, a daily lesson objective cannot really stand apart from the knowing minds before us in the classroom. The objective exists precisely as an object for students’ understanding. In this sense, the objective and the learner belong together.

For public charter schools, they are a real obligation and, at their best, can hold schools accountable to a baseline of shared competence. But they should function as a floor, not a ceiling. A standard may say that students should identify a main idea, solve a type of equation, or explain a historical cause. It cannot finally tell us why a text stirs the soul, what order mathematics reveals, or how history might teach humility and judgment.

A good lesson begins not with an abstract statement, but with a concrete encounter: a beautiful sentence, a mathematical problem, a historical image, a scientific phenomenon, a story. Classical pedagogy begins with the particular thing itself and moves from there toward the universal. Students are trained, over time, to attend, notice, wonder, ask, and then understand and name. If we announce, “Today you will identify the theme of sacrificial friendship,” we may flatten the very experience by which students might have come to see it. We have given away the punchline.
